name: The Zeigarnik Effect
statement: We remember what we left unfinished better than what we completed.
meaning: The Zeigarnik effect is the proposed tendency to remember interrupted or incomplete tasks better than completed ones. The unfinished sits in the mind and nags; the finished is let go. It is one of the most repeated ideas in popular psychology — though, as it turns out, one of the least reliably supported.
mechanism: The explanation comes from Kurt Lewin's field theory, in whose circle the effect was studied. Beginning a task is said to create a task-specific psychological tension, a quasi-need within the person's mental field, that keeps the task's contents accessible. Completing the task discharges the tension; interrupting it leaves the tension unresolved, so the material stays more available to memory. The traditional origin story has Lewin noticing that a waiter recalled unpaid orders sharply but forgot them once the bill was settled — an anecdote repeated everywhere but not itself documented data.

examples.text: An unresolved storyline keeps viewers turning it over between episodes — the most cited application, though an illustration rather than a controlled finding.
A task left half-done tends to intrude on the mind and press to be resumed, the everyday experience the effect is meant to name.
Zeigarnik had participants perform tasks, interrupting some, and reported better recall of the interrupted ones — the study that gave the effect its name.

variants.name: The Ovsiankina effect
variants.text: Maria Ovsiankina's related finding, from 1928, that people tend to resume an interrupted task when given the chance — a distinct phenomenon about doing rather than remembering, and one that replicates better.

variants.name: Tension in field theory
variants.text: Lewin's account of a quasi-need creating a state of tension that persists until a task is completed, the theoretical root of the effect.

whyItMatters: It has been enormously influential in psychology and beyond, invoked to explain everything from cliffhangers to study habits to intrusive worry. Its later history is a cautionary tale about how a memorable idea can outrun its evidence: the effect is a case study in fragile findings, worth knowing as much for its shaky replication record as for its original claim.

working.text: beginning a task can create a pull to return to it, so making a start is sometimes the best way to keep it in mind.
invoke the effect knowing its replication record is mixed to poor, not as an established law of memory.
distinguish the fragile memory claim from the better-supported tendency to resume interrupted tasks.

limits: The effect is empirically fragile and must not be presented as settled. Early replications were inconsistent, and a 1964 review found completed tasks were sometimes remembered better. It is highly condition-dependent, sensitive to motivation and ego-involvement, the perceived intentionality of the interruption, and whether the task seems feasible. A 2025 meta-analysis found no overall memory advantage for unfinished tasks — a weighted recall ratio essentially at parity — and concluded the effect lacks universal validity. Tellingly, the same analysis found the related Ovsiankina resumption effect does replicate, so the urge to resume holds up where the memory advantage does not.
misreadings: It is not a robust, well-established law of memory; its replication is mixed to poor, and a recent meta-analysis finds no overall advantage for unfinished tasks. The waiter story is the traditional origin, not experimental evidence. And remembering unfinished tasks must not be conflated with the urge to resume them — different phenomena with very different support, the resumption effect being the sturdier one.
origin: Named for Bluma Zeigarnik, a Lithuanian-Soviet psychologist, from her 1927 study 'Uber das Behalten von erledigten und unerledigten Handlungen' in Kurt Lewin's circle; its fragile replication record was underscored by a 2025 meta-analysis by Ghibellini and Meier.

sources.text: Zeigarnik, "Uber das Behalten von erledigten und unerledigten Handlungen," Psychologische Forschung 9:1-85 (1927), archived English translation. — the original interrupted-task experiments.

Ghibellini & Meier, "Interruption, recall and resumption: a meta-analysis of the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina effects," Humanities and Social Sciences Communications 12:962 (2025). — no overall memory advantage for unfinished tasks; the resumption effect replicates.
Zeigarnik effect, Wikipedia. — the statement, the Lewin field-theory mechanism, the waiter anecdote, and the mixed replication history.
